newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG voters to have their say on mercenary scandal.
newsitem.headline: PNG voters to have their say on mercenary scandal.

text.p: Papua New Guinea on Saturday begins the most important election of its short independent history, giving voters their first say since a mercenary scandal thrust the nation onto the world stage.

Elections in the South Pacific nation of 4.3 million people are normally only remarkable for the frankness with which candidates offer to buy votes in a land where pork-barrelling literally means gifts of pigs.

But this time voters will be asked to judge a government almost toppled by a civil and military crisis in March over a failed US$36 million plan to hire mercenaries to put down a nine-year secessionist rebellion on one of its island provinces.
Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan stood aside while an inquiry was conducted into the mercenary affair and resumed office last week saying he had been cleared of any wrongdoing.

Chan maintains he will not suffer at the polls from the plan to hire the mercenaries through London-based military consultancy Sandline International to quell the uprising on Bougainville, 800 kms (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.
He told reporters during campaigning this week in the country's rugged and remote Highlands that decisions often had to be made which did not win immediate approval.
"You have to make a tough decision, the right decision, and then people fall into line," Chan said.
Voting will last two weeks to give members of remote villages time to travel to polling stations, while counting is expected to take another week.

The revolving door of Papuan politics means Chan will be challenged by two former prime ministers, Paias Wingti and Sir Michael Somare, both of whom have held the office twice since the country won independence from nearby Australia in 1975.
Also running against Chan are finance minister Chris Haiveta, who signed the contract with Sandline, and former deputy prime minister Ted Diro.
Party politics have little relevance and the prime minister is chosen by a vote from the floor of the 109-member parliament.
Candidiates are often unwilling to tie themselves to a party and run as independents in the hope of cutting a deal with one of the winning coalition parties after the election.

This year's poll has attracted 2,368 candidates, 1,665 of them independents. Many seats have more than 20 candidates and one has attracted 61 nominations, meaning it could be won with only a few percent of the vote.
Turnover of ministers often reaches 50 percent, with some analysts tipping up to 80 percent of sitting members will not be returned this time under the first-past-the-post system.
Tribal loyalties are deeply ingrained in Papua New Guinea, where 85 percent of voters live in villages and are more likely to be swayed by the traditional culture of the "big man" than by policies.

"The deciding factor on winning for any candidate is really his personality, his credibility in the local society, whether he has a strong village or tribe, and on local issues," Wingti told reporters during campaigning.
It is also common for successful independent members to have their election expenses subsidised by coalitions in return for their vote on the floor of parliament.
"I do not call that corruption. I simply say they are independent, they've spent that money," Chan said.
In other areas the gift of a pig from a candidate seeking votes is the ultimate symbol of prestige and wealth.

Campaigning can also be as brutal as it is colourful in the country's 19 regions, where rallies can attract up to 10,000 voters including dancers wearing traditional head-dress made of exotic bird of paradise feathers.

A local newspaper reported in May that a supporter of a rival candidate had attempted to spear an MP from one Highlands seat. Another supporter was reported to have lost his testicles in the ensuing brawl.
